## A Thursday afternoon with the tea trolley

I retired after 41 years of bookkeeping, most of them at a builders’ merchant in Dereham. For the first few months I enjoyed having nowhere in particular to be. After that, I drifted a bit. I had no regular reason to go out most weeks, and the days had a habit of looking much the same.

I started volunteering at Wensum Vale Hospice in March 2022, about eighteen months after I retired. These days, every other Thursday afternoon, you’ll find me with the tea trolley in the day therapy unit. It has given me a reason to get out of the house, and I’m glad of it.

If you haven’t been into the day unit, you might imagine it’s a quiet or sombre place. On a Thursday it is mostly noisy and rather jolly. Around 14 to 18 patients come in, some for the art group or a hand massage, others for a bit of company. Most go home afterwards.

There are sad days, of course, and some weeks are hard. The staff look after us when that happens. But there is plenty of laughter too, sometimes at my expense.

In my first week I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much she had to be given a tissue. She told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. I was less pleased about the milk, but it broke the ice.

Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week. The story is slightly different each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. The bourbon biscuits are another reliable feature of Thursday afternoons: they always go first, so we now hide a packet for the late group.

You don’t need any nursing skills to do this. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what and listen. As it turns out, 41 years of keeping ledgers straight is quite handy when it comes to remembering the teas.

There are four of us on a rota meant for six. Two volunteers left over the summer: one moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, and the other had a knee operation. We’d be very pleased to welcome a couple more people.

The commitment is **one Thursday afternoon a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm**. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, does the induction, which takes about two hours. There is also a short online food hygiene course, paid for by the hospice.

If you’re curious, there’s a **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There’ll be tea and biscuits, and no obligation to sign up. Bring a friend if you like—we do have two places to fill. Or you can ring Bridget on the volunteering line for a chat.

You needn’t be saintly. I’m certainly not. It helps if you know where we’ve hidden the bourbons, though.
